text.en: People once travelled on foot, with bullocks, horses and camels. Now we use cycles, cars, trains, ships and aeroplanes. Even spacecraft go beyond the Earth.

The book tells us how far a person can usually travel in one hour. On foot it is about 3 to 5 km. On a cycle it is 12 to 20 km, by motorbike 40 to 60 km and by train 40 to 160 km.
By ship it is 25 to 45 km an hour and by aeroplane 750 to 920 km. A spacecraft travels at least 28,000 km in an hour.
So distances in an hour range from one-digit to five-digit numbers. Big numbers help us tell these stories.
A cyclist who covers 15 km in one hour covers 15 x 4 = 60 km in four hours, if she keeps the same speed.
To plan a trip for 461 girls and 439 boys, first add: 461 + 439 = 900 children. Then divide by the number of seats in each vehicle, for example 900 / 25 = 36 minibuses.
The chapter also teaches rounding with a hungry rabbit at 2,346. The nearest ten is 2,350, the nearest hundred is 2,300 and the nearest thousand is 2,000.
Look for large numbers around you: a book of 200 pages with about 50 words on a page has about 10,000 words in all.
(additional, not in the textbook) We usually measure distances in the sea and in the air in nautical miles, but in this class we use 1 km = 1,000 m.

problem.en: A cyclist covers 15 km in one hour. How far in 4 hours?

text.en: Distance in one hour is 15 km.

prompt.en: Explain how to find how many minibuses of 25 seats are needed for 900 people.

requiredIdeas.en: If something is left over we need one more vehicle

points.en: Different vehicles cover different distances in one hour.
Big numbers help us talk about travel and counts.
Rounding gives the nearest ten, hundred or thousand.
